definitions.text: to ask for a job, usually by writing a letter.
to be removed from a job, usually because you have done something bad.

definitions.text: to stop work and take a pension, usually when you are in late middle age.
to write in the empty spaces on a form.

task_2_nouns.title: Task 2. NOUNS
task_2_nouns.instruction: Fill in the gaps with an appropriate word from the box.
task_2_nouns.text:
A computer company had a (1) vacancy for position of (2) salesman, and decided to advertise for a new (3) employee. A lot of (4) applicants with good (5) qualifications and (6) experience applied for the job, and after all the interviews had finished, the directors made a (7) shortlist of the best (8) candidates then invited them to come back for another interview.
The person who eventually got the job was very happy. After all, he would receive an annual (9) salary of £25,000, with a 5% (10) pay rise twice a year, a 15% (11) commission for each computer he managed to sell, excellent (12) perks such as private health insurance and a company car, a company (13) pension to make sure he would be well-off when he retired, and the chance of (14) promotion from salesman to sales (15) manager if he was successful. All in all, his future (16) prospects looked very good.

rules.Can_and_Could: • Ability: Can denotes capability in the present tense (e.g., The current infrastructure can support the new application), whereas could signifies capability in the past tense (e.g., Previously, the department could solely rely on manual processing). To articulate future capability, the phrase will be able to is required rather than can (e.g., Following the upgrade, the server will be able to manage increased traffic).\n• Permission: Utilized to request or authorize permission concerning present or future actions (e.g., Authorized personnel can access the secure archives).\n• Possibility & Suggestions: Expresses potential options or theoretical possibilities in the present or future (e.g., Assuming sufficient capital is acquired, the organization can expand its facilities / The committee could consult an independent auditor prior to finalizing the fiscal report).
rules.May_and_Might:
• Possibility: Indicates that a circumstance is feasible in the present or future. May typically conveys a marginally higher degree of probability than might (e.g., Precipitation might occur tomorrow / The preliminary coordinates may be inaccurate).
• Permission: May is formally employed to grant or request authorization (e.g., Delegates may proceed to the designated conference hall).
• Optional Actions: Might serves to denote discretionary future actions (e.g., Should an individual miss the initial presentation, they might attend the supplementary session).
• Grammar Note: It is imperative to distinguish between the modal verb phrase may be and the adverb maybe (e.g., The physical document may be misfiled / Maybe the physical document is misfiled).
rules.Speculation_and_Deduction:
The integration of modal verbs with the auxiliary be facilitates deductive reasoning regarding present circumstances based on available evidence:
• High Certainty: Must be (e.g., The primary investigator is absent today; he must be unwell.)
• Moderate Certainty: Could be (e.g., The numerical discrepancy could be attributed to a systematic error.)
• Low Certainty: Might be (e.g., The observed anomaly might be a statistical outlier.)
• Negative Certainty: To assert that a hypothesis is definitively false, the constructions cannot be or could not be are utilized (e.g., The suspect departed mere moments ago; he cannot be far.).
rules.Obligation_and_Necessity:
• Must: Articulates a definitive obligation or necessity pertaining to the present or future (e.g., All personnel must adhere to established safety protocols).
• Must not (Mustn't): Imposes a strict prohibition against an action (e.g., Unauthorized data extraction must not occur in this sector).
• Have to / Had to: While semantically analogous to must, have to does not function grammatically as a modal verb. It is succeeded by an infinitive and possesses a distinct past tense formulation, had to, indicating historical obligations (e.g., It was necessary to submit the regulatory documentation yesterday; therefore, the team had to expedite the review process).
• Do not have to: Signifies an absence of obligation; the specified action is entirely discretionary (e.g., Attendance at the supplementary seminar is not mandatory; employees do not have to participate).
rules.Advice_and_Recommendations: • Should / Ought to: Employed to offer professional recommendations or counsel (e.g., It is recommended that researchers should rigorously verify their primary sources).\n• Negative Formulation: In standard professional discourse, should not is overwhelmingly preferred to the archaic ought not to.\n• Had better ('d better): Utilized to issue emphatic recommendations or advisories, frequently implying negative operational or strategic consequences for non-compliance (e.g., The administration had better address the infrastructural vulnerabilities, or significant operational delays will ensue).
rules.Would: • Past Intentions/Future in the Past: Applied to discuss past intentions or future events from a retrospective viewpoint. It functions as a more formal equivalent to was going to (e.g., The director indicated that he would independently review the proposal).\n• Polite Offers and Requests: The phrasing would like is universally applied to formulate courteous and professional requests, establishing a clear distinction from general declarations of preference (e.g., I would like to formally request an extension for the project deadline).\n• Past Habits: Illustrates habitual or recurring actions executed in the past (e.g., During previous fiscal years, the organization would routinely allocate surplus funds to research and development initiatives).

rules.Section 1: Modal Verbs - General Formati:
Modal verbs function as auxiliary components that accompany a principal verb to articulate concepts including ability, permission, obligation, prohibition, necessity, requests, offers, invitations, speculation, and counsel.
Common Modal Verbs: can, could, may, might, must, should, ought to, would.

General Rules for Formation:
• Base Form: Modal verbs are invariably succeeded by the base form of the principal verb (the infinitive excluding the particle to).
  - Correct: The software can process data rapidly.
  - Incorrect: The software can to process data rapidly.
• No Inflections: Inflections such as -s, -ed, or -ing must not be appended to modal verbs or the subsequent base verbs.
  - Correct: The system could handle significant data loads.
  - Incorrect: The system could handles / The system canned handle.
• Negatives: Negative constructions are formed by inserting the adverb not or its contracted form -n't directly following the modal verb (e.g., cannot, should not, could not). It should be noted that cannot is formally written as a single word.
• Questions: Interrogative structures require the inversion of the subject and the modal verb. The auxiliary verbs do, does, or did are strictly prohibited when formulating questions or negative statements involving modals.
  - Correct: Can the proposed model accommodate these variables?
  - Incorrect: Does the proposed model can accommodate these variables?
rules.Section 1.1: Modal Verbs - Can and Could:
• Ability: Can denotes capability in the present tense, whereas could signifies capability in the past tense.
  - Present: The current infrastructure can support the new application.
  - Past: Previously, the department could solely rely on manual processing.
  - Note regarding Future Tense: To articulate future capability, the phrase will be able to is required rather than can (e.g., Following the upgrade, the server will be able to manage increased traffic).
• Permission: Utilized to request or authorize permission concerning present or future actions.
  - Example: Authorized personnel can access the secure archives.
• Possibility & Suggestions: Expresses potential options or theoretical possibilities in the present or future.
  - Example: Assuming sufficient capital is acquired, the organization can expand its facilities.
  - Example: The committee could consult an independent auditor prior to finalizing the fiscal report.
rules.Section 1.2: Modal Verbs - May and Might:
• Possibility: Indicates that a circumstance is feasible in the present or future. May typically conveys a marginally higher degree of probability than might.
  - Example: Precipitation might occur tomorrow. / The preliminary coordinates may be inaccurate.
• Permission: May is formally employed to grant or request authorization.
  - Example: Delegates may proceed to the designated conference hall.
• Optional Actions: Might serves to denote discretionary future actions.
  - Example: Should an individual miss the initial presentation, they might attend the supplementary session.
• Grammar Note: It is imperative to distinguish between the modal verb phrase may be and the adverb maybe.
  - Modal: The physical document may be misfiled.
  - Adverb: Maybe the physical document is misfiled.
rules.Section 1.3: Modal Verbs - Speculation a:
The integration of modal verbs with the auxiliary be facilitates deductive reasoning regarding present circumstances based on available evidence:
• High Certainty: Must be (e.g., The primary investigator is absent today; he must be unwell.)
• Moderate Certainty: Could be (e.g., The numerical discrepancy could be attributed to a systematic error.)
• Low Certainty: Might be (e.g., The observed anomaly might be a statistical outlier.)
• Negative Certainty: To assert that a hypothesis is definitively false, the constructions cannot be or could not be are utilized (e.g., The suspect departed mere moments ago; he cannot be far.).
rules.Section 1.4: Modal Verbs - Obligation an:
• Must: Articulates a definitive obligation or necessity pertaining to the present or future.
  - Example: All personnel must adhere to established safety protocols.
• Must not (Mustn't): Imposes a strict prohibition against an action.
  - Example: Unauthorized data extraction must not occur in this sector.
• Have to / Had to: While semantically analogous to must, have to does not function grammatically as a modal verb. It is succeeded by an infinitive and possesses a distinct past tense formulation, had to, indicating historical obligations.
  - Example: It was necessary to submit the regulatory documentation yesterday; therefore, the team had to expedite the review process.
• Do not have to: Signifies an absence of obligation; the specified action is entirely discretionary.
  - Example: Attendance at the supplementary seminar is not mandatory; employees do not have to participate.
rules.Section 1.5: Modal Verbs - Advice and Re:
• Should / Ought to: Employed to offer professional recommendations or counsel.
  - Example: It is recommended that researchers should rigorously verify their primary sources.
  - Negative Formulation: In standard professional discourse, should not is overwhelmingly preferred to the archaic ought not to.
• Had better ('d better): Utilized to issue emphatic recommendations or advisories, frequently implying negative operational or strategic consequences for non-compliance.
  - Example: The administration had better address the infrastructural vulnerabilities, or significant operational delays will ensue.
rules.Section 1.6: Modal Verbs - Would:
• Past Intentions/Future in the Past: Applied to discuss past intentions or future events from a retrospective viewpoint. It functions as a more formal equivalent to was going to.
  - Example: The director indicated that he would independently review the proposal.
• Polite Offers and Requests: The phrasing would like is universally applied to formulate courteous and professional requests, establishing a clear distinction from general declarations of preference.
  - Request: I would like to formally request an extension for the project deadline.
  - Preference: I favor extended project deadlines.
• Past Habits: Illustrates habitual or recurring actions executed in the past.
  - Example: During previous fiscal years, the organization would routinely allocate surplus funds to research and development initiatives.
rules.Section 2: Adverbs of Time (Still, Alrea:
• Still: Denotes the continuation of a circumstance, frequently exceeding anticipated temporal parameters.
  - Placement: Positioned mid-sentence. It precedes the principal verb but follows the verb be. In instances involving multi-word verbs, it is placed subsequent to the initial auxiliary verb. When modifying a negative verb, still must precede the negation.
  - Example: Does the methodology remain confusing? / The core principles are still ambiguous to the trainees.
• Already: Signifies that an event has transpired prior to projected timelines.
  - Placement: Positioned mid-sentence, adhering to the identical placement conventions as still within affirmative structures.
  - Example: The regulatory board has already issued its preliminary findings.
• Yet: Implies an anticipation of a forthcoming occurrence. This adverb features predominantly in negative constructs and interrogative sentences.
  - Placement: Typically positioned at the conclusion of the clause or sentence.
  - Example: Has the auditing process not concluded yet? / The preliminary data has not been fully processed yet.
rules.Section 3: Expressing Opinions and Struc:
1. Contrasting Ideas
• On the one hand / On the other hand: Employed concurrently to juxtapose divergent perspectives or conflicting data regarding a singular scenario.
  - Example: On the one hand, the proposed intervention offers significant theoretical benefits. On the other hand, it presents substantial logistical challenges.
• On the contrary: Serves to assert the direct antithesis of a preceding proposition.
  - Example: The current regulations are not unduly restrictive. On the contrary, they provide unprecedented operational flexibility.

2. Stating Opinions
• In my opinion: Functions as a marker for subjective viewpoints, clearly delineating personal analysis from objective fact. (The phrasing "According to me" is grammatically invalid and must be stringently avoided).
  - Example: In my professional assessment, allocating capital to that specific sector carries substantial financial risk.
• According to: Employed to reference external perspectives, cite secondary sources, or attribute statements to specific individuals or organizations.
  - Example: According to recent epidemiological studies, the incidence rate has plateaued.

3. Sequencing and Timing
• Firstly / First of all: Serves to establish the primary assertion within a logical argument or enumeration.
  - Example: Firstly, it is crucial to delineate the parameters of the investigation.
• At first: Delineates the initial phase of a circumstance, frequently preceding an adversative conjunction (such as but) to indicate subsequent developmental alterations.
  - Example: At first, the initial trials yielded inconclusive results, but subsequent iterations demonstrated clear and measurable efficacy.
rules.Section 4: Hope vs. Wish:
The verbs hope and wish articulate desires concerning states of affairs; however, their grammatical application diverges significantly based on the probability of the desired outcome.
• Hope (Indicating Feasibility): Utilized for future or present scenarios that remain plausible, attainable, or mathematically probable.
  - Example: The executive committee hopes to finalize the strategic plan by the upcoming quarter.
• Wish + Past Tense (Indicating Present Impossibility): Applied to situations that are currently unfeasible or directly contrary to established reality.
  - Example: The principal investigator wishes the laboratory had greater analytical capacity. (Reality: The capacity is currently restricted).
• Wish + Past Perfect (Indicating Historical Regret): Employed to convey regret regarding past events or decisions that can no longer be altered.
  - Example: Management wishes the operational flaw had been identified prior to the product launch. (Reality: The flaw was not identified).
• Wish + Would (Indicating Desired Behavioral Modification): Functions to express professional dissatisfaction with ongoing behavioral patterns and a distinct desire for an entity or individual to alter their conduct.
  - Example: The advisory board wishes the contracting agency would adhere more strictly to the stipulated deadlines.

rules.Can and Could:
• Ability: Can denotes capability in the present tense, whereas could signifies capability in the past tense.
  - Present: The current infrastructure can support the new application.
  - Past: Previously, the department could solely rely on manual processing.
  - Note regarding Future Tense: To articulate future capability, the phrase will be able to is required rather than can (e.g., Following the upgrade, the server will be able to manage increased traffic).
• Permission: Utilized to request or authorize permission concerning present or future actions.
  - Example: Authorized personnel can access the secure archives.
• Possibility & Suggestions: Expresses potential options or theoretical possibilities in the present or future.
  - Example: Assuming sufficient capital is acquired, the organization can expand its facilities.
  - Example: The committee could consult an independent auditor prior to finalizing the fiscal report.

rules.May and Might:
• Possibility: Indicates that a circumstance is feasible in the present or future. May typically conveys a marginally higher degree of probability than might.
  - Example: Precipitation might occur tomorrow. / The preliminary coordinates may be inaccurate.
• Permission: May is formally employed to grant or request authorization.
  - Example: Delegates may proceed to the designated conference hall.
• Optional Actions: Might serves to denote discretionary future actions.
  - Example: Should an individual miss the initial presentation, they might attend the supplementary session.
• Grammar Note: It is imperative to distinguish between the modal verb phrase may be and the adverb maybe.
  - Modal: The physical document may be misfiled.
  - Adverb: Maybe the physical document is misfiled.

rules.Speculation and Deduction (Must be, Coul:
The integration of modal verbs with the auxiliary be facilitates deductive reasoning regarding present circumstances based on available evidence:
• High Certainty: Must be (e.g., The primary investigator is absent today; he must be unwell.)
• Moderate Certainty: Could be (e.g., The numerical discrepancy could be attributed to a systematic error.)
• Low Certainty: Might be (e.g., The observed anomaly might be a statistical outlier.)
• Negative Certainty: To assert that a hypothesis is definitively false, the constructions cannot be or could not be are utilized (e.g., The suspect departed mere moments ago; he cannot be far.).

rules.Obligation and Necessity (Must and Have:
• Must: Articulates a definitive obligation or necessity pertaining to the present or future.
  - Example: All personnel must adhere to established safety protocols.
• Must not (Mustn't): Imposes a strict prohibition against an action.
  - Example: Unauthorized data extraction must not occur in this sector.
• Have to / Had to: While semantically analogous to must, have to does not function grammatically as a modal verb. It is succeeded by an infinitive and possesses a distinct past tense formulation, had to, indicating historical obligations.
  - Example: It was necessary to submit the regulatory documentation yesterday; therefore, the team had to expedite the review process.
• Do not have to: Signifies an absence of obligation; the specified action is entirely discretionary.
  - Example: Attendance at the supplementary seminar is not mandatory; employees do not have to participate.

rules.Advice and Recommendations (Should, Ough:
• Should / Ought to: Employed to offer professional recommendations or counsel.
  - Example: It is recommended that researchers should rigorously verify their primary sources.
  - Negative Formulation: In standard professional discourse, should not is overwhelmingly preferred to the archaic ought not to.
• Had better ('d better): Utilized to issue emphatic recommendations or advisories, frequently implying negative operational or strategic consequences for non-compliance.
  - Example: The administration had better address the infrastructural vulnerabilities, or significant operational delays will ensue.

rules.Would:
• Past Intentions/Future in the Past: Applied to discuss past intentions or future events from a retrospective viewpoint. It functions as a more formal equivalent to was going to.
  - Example: The director indicated that he would independently review the proposal.
• Polite Offers and Requests: The phrasing would like is universally applied to formulate courteous and professional requests, establishing a clear distinction from general declarations of preference.
  - Request: I would like to formally request an extension for the project deadline.
  - Preference: I favor extended project deadlines.
• Past Habits: Illustrates habitual or recurring actions executed in the past.
  - Example: During previous fiscal years, the organization would routinely allocate surplus funds to research and development initiatives.
